newsitem.title: UK: Dublin calls for peace at coming N.Irish marches.
newsitem.headline: Dublin calls for peace at coming N.Irish marches.

text.p: Ireland said on Tuesday Britain's decision to permit the flashpoint Protestant parade in Northern Ireland last weekend showed "might is right" and appealed for peace to prevail at more planned marches.

Irish Foreign Minister Ray Burke made the comments after talks with Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary Mo Mowlam, who faced mounting Catholic anger over a leaked official document which suggested she had ignored their objections.
"Our concern of course is that historically all of these decisions are that might is right and that is on the Orange side," Burke told reporters.
He said he did not want to "rake over what has happened" but appealed to the Protestant Orange Order to "see the wisdom of peace this weekend rather than just the right to march".

"I hope Orange marchers will see there is a counter-right for people not to be intimidated in their own homes," said Burke, referring to parades planned for the Lower Ormeau Road in Belfast and in Londonderry on Saturday.

The latest multi-party talks, sponsored by Britain and Ireland, were overshadowed by some of the worst violence in Northern Ireland for years, ignited by Catholic anger over the routing of an Orange Order parade through a Catholic area of Portadown.

Mowlam was at the centre of controversy after the leaked document was interpreted as meaning that her officials had decided weeks before the parade that it would have to go ahead as "the least worst option" despite bitter Catholic opposition.

She said Nationalist groups on the Ormeau road were no longer talking to her because of the Portadown decision, complicating her efforts to find an agrement to avoid confrontation on the Lower Ormeau Road next Saturday.
"Nationalists are very angry. Nationalists are thinking about whether to talk to me or not, so my use may be limited after my failure in Garvaghy. I accept that," Mowlam said.

John Hume, leader of the mainstream Catholic Social Democratic and Labour Party, called for a moratorium on all marches, something unlikely to find much support among Orangemen as they approach the high point of the annual "marching season".

"We have very strong anger to express. We believe that what has happened is intensifying the tensions in our community and those tensions, unfortunately as we know, have in the past given rise to confrontation and to violence on our streets," he said.
Hume's deputy Seamus Mallon added: "Those who are trying hardest to get a solution to this problem have a right to feel very deeply hurt."
Nationalist anger was inflamed by a reference in the leaked document to the best means of "getting some Orange feet on the Garvaghy Road".

That march last weekend plunged Northern Ireland into the worst outbreak of Catholic, Irish nationalist anger for years, in which more than a hundred people have been injured in nightly riots and scores of bullets fired by IRA guerrillas.

The coming weekend's parades mark July 12, the most hallowed date in the Orange Order's calendar, commemorating a 1690 victory by a Protestant King over an invading Catholic monarch which assured that a Protestant came to the throne in London.
Mowlam denied the implication of the leaked document that her advisers decided on June 20 to permit the last Orange Order march, 15 days before a decision was announced and greeted by riots.
The embattled British minister said the Northern Ireland Office document was merely a summary of options drawn up by security advisers.
